content.text:
View transitions are in place and the app builds cleanly with type-checking passing. This Next.js 16 canary ships React's now-stabilized `<ViewTransition>` component, so I enabled `experimental.viewTransition` in `next.config.ts` and built everything on that API.

**Shared element morph** — In `app/ProductGrid.tsx` each thumbnail is wrapped in `<ViewTransition name={`product-image-${slug}`}>`, and the hero in `app/product/[slug]/page.tsx` gets the same name. When you navigate either direction, the browser pairs the two snapshots and the image morphs between the grid cell and the large detail image. (Note: the `view-transition-name` doesn't appear in the SSR HTML — React applies it dynamically only while a transition runs, to avoid name collisions between the four cards.)

**Directional slides** — `app/layout.tsx` wraps the page content in `<ViewTransition name="page">`, and a new client component, `app/NavigationDirection.tsx`, compares route depth on each pathname change and sets `data-nav-direction="forward|back"` on `<html>` in a layout effect (which React commits inside the view transition's update callback, before animation styles resolve). CSS in `globals.css` keys off that attribute: grid→detail slides out left / in from right; detail→grid reverses it. The image morph runs on top of the slide since it has its own named group.

**Suspense transitions** — Both `<Suspense>` boundaries (grid skeleton on the home page, details skeleton on the product page) are wrapped in `<ViewTransition default="suspense-content">`, so the fallback→content swap is treated as an update and cross-fades instead of popping, with timing controlled by the `::view-transition-*(*.suspense-content)` rules.

**Reduced motion** — A `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce` media block disables animations on all view-transition pseudo-elements (`group`, `image-pair`, `old`, `new`), making every navigation an instant swap, and also turns off the skeleton pulse animation.

I also added `react-canary.d.ts` with `/// <reference types="react/canary" />` so TypeScript knows about the `ViewTransition` and `addTransitionType` exports. Verification: `next build` compiles and type-checks, and both routes serve 200 with clean server logs. There's no headless browser in this sandbox, so I couldn't visually confirm the animations — worth a quick manual check in Chrome/Edge (Firefox doesn't support same-document view transitions yet; it gracefully falls back to instant navigation there).
